title: Rousseau: The Social Contract and the General Will
subtitle: Civilisation made us clever, vain and unequal; can politics make us free again?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain why the 'noble savage' label misrepresents Rousseau's actual view of natural humanity
Distinguish amour de soi from amour-propre and explain how Rousseau thinks inequality arose
Explain the problem The Social Contract sets out to solve and Rousseau's solution through the general will
Distinguish the general will from the will of all, and evaluate the worry about being 'forced to be free'
Describe the aims of Emile and the main criticisms of Rousseau's legacy
hook:
On a hot afternoon in 1749, a struggling music copyist in his late thirties was walking the road from Paris to the fortress of Vincennes, where his friend Denis Diderot was imprisoned for writing an irreligious book. To rest, he sat under a tree and glanced at a newspaper. It announced a prize essay competition from the Academy of Dijon: Has the restoration of the sciences and arts contributed to the purification of morals?

As he later described it, he was overwhelmed by a sudden flood of insight so intense that he felt dizzy and wept without noticing. He saw, he said, that humans are naturally good, and that it is our institutions alone that make us bad. The man was Jean-Jacques Rousseau. He answered the Academy's question with a resounding no, won the prize, and became overnight the most provocative voice of the Enlightenment: a thinker who used Enlightenment reason to question whether all its progress had made us better at all.

sections.heading: The Citizen of Geneva
sections.body:
Rousseau was born in 1712 in Geneva, then a small, self-governing Protestant republic. His mother died days after his birth. His father, a watchmaker, raised him on romantic novels and Plutarch's lives of heroic Greeks and Romans, then left Geneva after a quarrel when Jean-Jacques was ten. Apprenticed to an engraver, the teenager ran away at fifteen, after finding the city gates locked one evening, and wandered for years. He converted to Catholicism, became the protégé and later lover of a woman named Madame de Warens, and educated himself by voracious reading.

In Paris in the 1740s he became friends with Diderot and contributed articles on music to the great *Encyclopédie* (Day 54). He was gifted, awkward, proud and increasingly suspicious of others. The prize essay of 1750, the *Discourse on the Sciences and Arts*, made him famous. It argued that the polish of civilisation, its manners, luxury and learning, had covered human beings in garlands of flowers while concealing their chains, encouraging vanity and hypocrisy rather than virtue.

He proudly signed his works 'Citizen of Geneva' and admired the ideal, if not the reality, of a small republic of engaged citizens. Remember Machiavelli's love of the Roman republic in the *Discourses* (Day 39). Rousseau drew on the same tradition of civic virtue.

His life also contains a fact he himself confessed and that his enemies never let him forget. He and his partner Thérèse Levasseur had five children, and Rousseau placed every one of them in the Paris foundling hospital, where most infants died. He later described this in his autobiography, the *Confessions*, with a mixture of justification and remorse. The man who wrote the most influential book on education of his century abandoned his own children. Readers have argued ever since about what, if anything, that should mean for his ideas.

sections.heading: Natural Man: Not a Noble Savage
sections.body:
Rousseau is often said to have praised the **noble savage** and wanted us to return to nature. Both claims are wrong. The phrase 'noble savage' does not appear in Rousseau; it comes from John Dryden's play *The Conquest of Granada* (1670). The anthropologist Ter Ellingson has argued that its association with Rousseau was largely constructed by nineteenth-century writers. And Rousseau explicitly said that we cannot return to the forests to live with bears.

His real view is subtler. In the *Discourse on the Origin of Inequality* (1755), his entry for another Dijon competition (which this time he did not win), he criticises Hobbes and Locke (Days 42 and 52) for making the same mistake: they describe 'natural' humans who already think, compete and own things like seventeenth-century Englishmen. Hobbes's war of all against all assumes pride and rivalry; Locke's state of nature already has property. Rousseau tries to strip away everything society added.

What is left is a creature that is solitary, healthy, largely self-sufficient and moved by two pre-rational principles: **amour de soi**, a natural concern for one's own preservation and well-being, and **pity**, a natural repugnance at seeing another sentient being suffer. Natural man is not morally virtuous, since he has no ideas of justice or virtue at all. He is, rather, innocent: neither good nor evil in the moral sense, and not inclined to harm others when he does not need to.

What distinguishes humans from other animals, Rousseau argues, is not mainly reason but freedom and **perfectibility**: the capacity to develop and change ourselves. This is the source of all our achievements, and also of all our misery. Perfectibility is what drew us out of our innocent condition and into a history of growing complexity, comparison and dependence.

sections.heading: Amour-Propre and the Birth of Inequality
sections.body:
How did we get from innocence to the world Rousseau saw around him, a world of kings and beggars? His *Second Discourse* tells a conjectural history, a story of what might plausibly have happened rather than a record of what did.

As humans began to live near one another, in huts and families and then small communities, something new emerged. People started to look at each other and wanted to be looked at. Whoever sang or danced best, the most handsome, the strongest, the most skilful, came to be the most highly regarded. And this, Rousseau writes, was the first step toward inequality and, at the same time, toward vice.

This new passion is **amour-propre**: self-love that depends on comparison and on how we appear in others' eyes. Unlike amour de soi, which is satisfied when our real needs are met, amour-propre can never be satisfied, because it is relative. It is not enough for me to do well; I must do better than you, and be seen to. Amour-propre drives envy, vanity, competition and the desire to dominate. Above all, it makes us live outside ourselves, in the opinion of others.

The decisive step came with agriculture, metallurgy and private property. In one of the most famous paragraphs of the century, Rousseau writes that the first man who, having enclosed a piece of ground, took it into his head to say this is mine, and found people simple enough to believe him, was the true founder of civil society. How many crimes, wars, murders and horrors, he adds, would have been spared the human race by someone who pulled up the stakes and cried out: do not listen to this impostor; you are lost if you forget that the fruits of the earth belong to all and the earth to no one.

Finally, Rousseau suggests, the rich, fearing for their possessions, proposed to the poor a deceptive social contract: let us unite to protect everyone from oppression. Everyone ran towards their chains, believing they were securing their freedom. Laws and government thus fixed inequality into permanent form. Compare Locke's account of property from yesterday: the very same story of enclosure and labour, told as a tragedy instead of a triumph.

sections.heading: Born Free, Everywhere in Chains
sections.body:
If the *Second Discourse* is a diagnosis, *The Social Contract* (1762) is an attempted cure. It opens with one of the most famous sentences in political philosophy:

> Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.

Rousseau then surprises the reader. He does not say how to break the chains. He asks instead what could make them legitimate. Since we cannot go back to nature, the question is whether there can be a form of political association in which we remain as free as before.

He states the problem precisely: to find a form of association which defends and protects with the whole common force the person and goods of each associate, and in which each, while uniting with all, nevertheless obeys only himself and remains as free as before.

His solution is the **social contract**: each of us puts his person and all his power in common under the supreme direction of the **general will**, and the body receives each member as an indivisible part of the whole. Unlike Hobbes's subjects, who hand power to a sovereign above them, Rousseau's citizens together are the **sovereign**. Because each gives himself entirely, and on equal terms, no one has an interest in making the conditions burdensome for others.

What do we gain? Rousseau says we lose natural liberty, the unlimited right to anything we can get, and gain **civil liberty**, limited by the general will, and property secured by law. Most importantly, we gain **moral liberty**, which alone makes us truly masters of ourselves: for the impulse of appetite alone is slavery, and obedience to the law one has prescribed for oneself is freedom. Kant (Day 56) will build his whole ethics on this idea of self-legislation, which he called autonomy.

sections.heading: The General Will and Being Forced to Be Free
sections.body:
What exactly is the **general will**? It is the will of the citizen body directed to the **common good**, the shared interests that every citizen has as a member of the community. Rousseau carefully distinguishes it from the **will of all**, which is merely the sum of private wills, each aiming at private interest. A majority vote in which each person asks 'what is best for me?' gives you the will of all. A vote in which each asks 'what is best for us all?' aims at the general will.

So the general will is not simply majority opinion. Rousseau thinks that under good conditions, when citizens are well informed, vote independently and are not divided into powerful factions, the majority will usually track it. That is why he distrusts organised parties and associations, which substitute group interests for the common good. It is also why he thinks the general will can only be expressed through general laws that apply equally to everyone, never through decrees aimed at particular people.

Rousseau was severe about representation. The English people, he wrote, think they are free, but they are free only during the election of members of Parliament; as soon as they are elected, the people are slaves. Sovereignty cannot be represented. He therefore imagined small republics, like an idealised Geneva, where citizens could assemble to make laws themselves.

Now the most controversial line. Whoever refuses to obey the general will, Rousseau writes, shall be compelled to do so by the whole body, which means nothing other than that **he will be forced to be free**. His thought is that a person who breaks a just law is enslaved to private appetite, and that compelling him restores him to the condition of a free citizen. But the phrase has chilled many readers. Who decides what the general will is? What if a government claims to know the true will of the people better than the people do?

Those fears seemed confirmed when the French revolutionaries, above all Robespierre, invoked Rousseau and the general will during the Terror of 1793–94. In the twentieth century, Isaiah Berlin counted Rousseau among the enemies of liberty, and J. L. Talmon traced 'totalitarian democracy' back to him. Defenders respond that Rousseau insisted on equality before law, distrusted concentrated power and cannot be blamed for those who used his words. He also proposed a **civil religion** of simple civic beliefs, and wrote that anyone who publicly acknowledged its dogmas and then behaved as if he did not believe them could be punished with death: a passage even admirers find hard to defend.

sections.heading: Emile and the Education of Natural Feeling
sections.body:
In the same year, 1762, Rousseau published *Emile, or On Education*, a long, part-novel, part-treatise following an imaginary boy raised by a tutor. Its first sentence sets the theme: everything is good as it leaves the hands of the Author of things; everything degenerates in the hands of man.

Rousseau's method is radical. Instead of drilling children in books and moral maxims, let them learn from experience, from things rather than words, at the pace of their own development. Protect the child from the corrupting influence of amour-propre for as long as possible. Teach a trade. Postpone abstract and religious instruction until the young man can understand it. The aim is a person who can live in society without being enslaved to its opinions. Its influence on later education, from Pestalozzi to child-centred schooling, was enormous.

But Book V, on Emile's future wife, Sophie, prescribes a very different education: girls are to be raised to please men, to be useful to them and to make their lives sweet. Mary Wollstonecraft will attack this directly on Day 54.

*Emile* also contained the 'Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar', a defence of natural religion based on conscience and feeling rather than revelation. Both *Emile* and *The Social Contract* were condemned and burned in Paris and in Geneva, and Rousseau fled arrest. He spent his last years moving between refuges, increasingly convinced of conspiracies against him, including a bitter quarrel with Hume, who had brought him to England in 1766. He died in 1778. In 1794 the revolutionary government moved his remains to the Panthéon in Paris, where they lie near those of his old enemy Voltaire.

keyQuote.text: Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.
keyQuote.source: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Social Contract (1762), Book I, Chapter 1

modernConnection.title: Amour-Propre with a Like Button
modernConnection.body:
Rousseau's description of the moment people began to look at each other and wanted to be looked at could serve as a description of social media.

Platforms built around likes, followers, views and shares turn amour-propre into a measurable, never-ending game. Their metrics are relative by design: a post is a success not because it meets a real need but because it outperforms others. Rousseau's diagnosis fits closely. Amour-propre can never be satisfied, because there is always someone with more followers. It makes us live outside ourselves, constantly imagining how we appear. And it breeds a culture of performance in which, as Rousseau complained of Parisian salons, people seem rather than are. Psychologists studying social comparison have found links between heavy social media use and envy and lower well-being, especially among teenagers, though how strong and how causal those links are is still debated.

Rousseau's political ideas are being tested too. Citizens' assemblies, groups of randomly selected ordinary people who hear evidence, deliberate and make recommendations, are a modern attempt to find something like the general will: citizens asking what is good for all rather than voting their private interest. Ireland's Citizens' Assembly (2016–18), whose recommendations helped prepare the way for the 2018 referendum on abortion, is a well-known example.

But be careful with the comparisons. Rousseau did not think amour-propre was simply bad; in *Emile* he hopes to educate it into a healthy desire for respect among equals, which suggests the problem is the form recognition takes, not the desire for it. And modern referendums and assemblies are not Rousseau's sovereign people making all laws directly. His warnings also cut against populist leaders who claim to speak for the true will of the people against its elected institutions: exactly the danger his critics saw in the phrase 'forced to be free'.

vocabulary.definition: Rousseau's term for natural, healthy self-love: concern for one's own preservation and well-being, which is satisfied when real needs are met.
vocabulary.example: Eating when hungry and resting when tired are expressions of amour de soi.

vocabulary.definition: Self-love that depends on comparison with others and on their opinion; for Rousseau, a source of vanity, envy and inequality.
vocabulary.example: Buying a car mainly to impress the neighbours is driven by amour-propre.

vocabulary.definition: Rousseau's term for the distinctively human capacity to develop and transform ourselves, the source of both progress and misery.
vocabulary.example: Our perfectibility let us invent agriculture and writing, and also war and slavery.

vocabulary.definition: The will of the citizen body directed towards the common good, which for Rousseau is the source of legitimate law.
vocabulary.example: A citizen who votes for a park she will rarely use because it benefits the whole town is aiming at the general will.

vocabulary.definition: The mere sum of individuals' private wills, each aimed at private interest; distinguished by Rousseau from the general will.
vocabulary.example: If every voter simply chooses the tax plan that saves them the most money, the result expresses the will of all.

vocabulary.definition: For Rousseau, the freedom of obeying a law one has prescribed for oneself, as opposed to being driven by appetite.
vocabulary.example: Keeping a promise you made to yourself, despite temptation, shows moral liberty.

vocabulary.definition: A stereotype of 'primitive' peoples as innocent and virtuous; often wrongly attributed to Rousseau, who never used the phrase.
vocabulary.example: Calling Rousseau the prophet of the noble savage ignores his view that we cannot return to nature.

vocabulary.definition: Rousseau's proposal for a minimal set of public religious beliefs that support citizenship, such as belief in God, an afterlife and the sanctity of the social contract.
vocabulary.example: Some sociologists describe national holidays and pledges of allegiance as a modern civil religion.

thinkingExercise.title: Audit Your Amour-Propre
thinkingExercise.prompt: Spend 10–15 minutes examining how much of your daily life is driven by comparison, then turn to politics.
steps: List five things you bought, did or posted in the last month. For each, ask: was this driven mainly by amour de soi (a real need or pleasure) or by amour-propre (how it would look to others)? Be honest.
Pick one item driven by amour-propre. Would you still want it if no one else could ever know you had it?
Now think of a recent public vote or political choice. Write down what you thought was best for you, and separately what you thought was best for everyone. Were they the same?

Rousseau says the general will is different from the will of all. Do you think a group of people really can aim at a common good, or is 'the common good' always someone's private interest in disguise? Write a short paragraph defending your answer.

summary: Rousseau (1712–1778) argued that humans are naturally innocent and that society's institutions corrupted them; he never praised the 'noble savage' or urged a return to nature.

Natural humans are moved by amour de soi and pity; social life breeds amour-propre, the comparative self-love behind vanity, envy and inequality, fixed in place by property and a deceptive contract of the rich.
The Social Contract asks how we can unite with others yet obey only ourselves; its answer is that citizens together form a sovereign directed by the general will.

The general will aims at the common good and differs from the will of all; Rousseau's claim that dissenters may be 'forced to be free' has been read as a seed of totalitarianism, a reading his defenders dispute.
Emile proposed a natural, experience-based education for boys but a subordinate one for girls; both major works of 1762 were burned, and Rousseau spent his last years in flight.

quiz.question: What is Rousseau's actual view of natural humanity?
options: Natural humans were noble, wise and morally virtuous, and we should return to that state
Natural humans were solitary and innocent, moved by self-preservation and pity, and we cannot return to that state
Natural humans lived in a war of all against all
Natural humans already owned property by mixing their labour with nature
quiz.explanation: Rousseau's natural humans are innocent rather than virtuous, and he denied that return was possible. The war of all against all is Hobbes's; natural property is Locke's.

quiz.question: Which situation best illustrates amour-propre?
options: Drinking water because you are thirsty
Helping a stranger who has fallen
Feeling crushed because a colleague's post received more likes than yours
Sleeping when you are tired
quiz.explanation: Amour-propre is self-love that depends on comparison and others' opinion. The first and last are amour de soi; the second is pity.

quiz.question: According to the Second Discourse, who was the true founder of civil society?
options: The first lawgiver who wrote down rules
The first king anointed by God
The first teacher who founded a school
The first person who enclosed land, said 'this is mine', and found people simple enough to believe him
quiz.explanation: For Rousseau, private property marked the decisive step into civil society, with all its inequalities.

quiz.question: What problem does The Social Contract set out to solve?
options: How to find an association that protects everyone while each, uniting with all, still obeys only himself and remains free
How to prove that kings rule by divine right
How to return humanity to the state of nature
How to maximise national wealth
quiz.explanation: Rousseau's 'fundamental problem' is to reconcile the protection of association with individual freedom.

quiz.question: How does the general will differ from the will of all?
options: The general will is the king's will; the will of all is Parliament's
The general will requires unanimity; the will of all requires a majority
The general will aims at the common good; the will of all is merely the sum of private interests
There is no difference; Rousseau used the terms interchangeably
quiz.explanation: Rousseau insists that adding up private interests does not by itself yield the common good.

quiz.question: What did Rousseau mean by moral liberty?
options: The right to do whatever one desires
Obedience to a law one has prescribed for oneself
Freedom from all laws and governments
The freedom of the rich to use their property as they wish
quiz.explanation: Being driven by appetite alone is slavery; giving oneself the law is freedom. Kant later built on this idea as autonomy.

quiz.question: Why did Rousseau argue that the English were free only during elections?
options: Because the English monarchy was absolute
Because English elections were rigged
Because the English had no written laws
Because sovereignty cannot be represented; once representatives are chosen, the people no longer make their own laws
quiz.explanation: Rousseau held that the people must legislate for themselves; handing that power to representatives surrenders it.

quiz.question: The phrase 'noble savage' was coined by Rousseau in the Discourse on the Origin of Inequality.
quiz.explanation: The phrase appears in Dryden's The Conquest of Granada (1670) and does not occur in Rousseau's writings.

quiz.question: Rousseau wrote that someone who refuses to obey the general will may be compelled to do so, which means he will be forced to be free.
quiz.explanation: This line from Book I of The Social Contract is among the most debated in political philosophy.

quiz.question: In Emile, Rousseau proposed that boys and girls receive exactly the same education.
quiz.explanation: Book V prescribes a very different education for Sophie, centred on pleasing and serving men, which Wollstonecraft attacked.

goDeeper.body:
Is Rousseau a friend or an enemy of liberty? The debate is one of the most heated in the history of political thought.

The prosecution was led in the mid-twentieth century by liberal thinkers who had watched totalitarian regimes claim to embody the true will of the people. Isaiah Berlin, in radio lectures published as *Freedom and Its Betrayal*, called Rousseau one of the most sinister and formidable enemies of liberty in modern thought, because he identified freedom with obeying a correct collective will. In his essay 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958), Berlin warned against 'positive' conceptions of freedom that let authorities claim to free us by coercing us.

The defence has been just as vigorous. Scholars such as Frederick Neuhouser, in *Rousseau's Theory of Self-Love* (2008), argue that Rousseau's central insight is about recognition: humans need the respect of others, and the political task is to channel amour-propre into equal standing among citizens rather than domination. On this reading, Rousseau is a profound theorist of why inequality damages everyone's psychology, and a forerunner of modern egalitarians. Rawls (Day 82) took Rousseau as one of the three great social contract theorists he wanted to build on, alongside Locke and Kant.

A third view sees Rousseau as a diagnostician rather than a planner. His real legacy, on this reading, is a series of critiques that run through Kant, Hegel (Day 59), Marx (Day 63) and the Romantic movement: civilisation alienates us from ourselves; progress in knowledge is not progress in goodness; inequality is made, not natural. Whether his cures work, his questions have proved impossible to ignore.

questions: Can amour-propre be educated into something healthy, or is the desire for recognition always dangerous?
Is there such a thing as a common good distinct from the sum of individual interests? How would we know what it is?
Rousseau abandoned his children yet wrote a revolutionary book on education. Should a philosopher's life affect how we judge their ideas?
